That is forcing things.

That certainly is forcing things. On page A-25 the minister will find a further payment to J. S. Neil & Sons, Fredericton, of $383, making a total of about $1,232 for explosives alone in clearing land at this experimental farm.
Are bees kept at the La-combe experimental farm?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
How long have they been kept there?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: For about one year.

I did not know that they were kept, and I desired to suggest that they should be added to the establishment, for this reason, that, while bees have been kept in Northern Alberta ever since 1888, the winter conditions there are so different from what they are in most countries where bees are kept that there are difficulties in successfully wintering them. For that reason very few private owners have taken up the industry. Some have, and some have been measurably successful. But, owing to the dangers of wintering, bee-keeping has been a matter of great uncertainty, which has prevented the extension of this industry. Flowers in summer are remarkably abundant in that country and there is a vast natural crop of honey. It is a pity not to utilize it. In addition to the native wild-flowers which are so remarkably abundant, the small white clover, which we sometimes call Dutch clover, has become very plentiful. It has a very short stem and grows in bunches. It only grows long enough for pasture. It is not indigenous, but it has become acclimatized, and it has spread to a marvellous de-

gree. This white clover is a tremendous producer of honey of the very highest quality; therefore, I think that the department would be well advised to take up the quesf-tion of bee culture at the Lacombe farm with a view of demonstrating the best means of keeping the bees safely throughout the winter. That is the great question, practically the only question, which has to be solved. It can be solved to better advantage by the skill, science and capital available to the Government on its farm than it could be by a private enterprise. Once that question is satisfactorily solved we may look for an enormous production of honey in that northern country, partly because of the wild-flowers, and partly because of the spread of the white clover.

Before six o'clock, the
minister stated that we might return to the item of Experimental Farms. I think the impression is growing in the country that the Experimental Farms are costing a good deal of money, and the question naturally arises, w'hether some of that money could not be saved, whether greater economy could not be practised, whether there is a close and proper supervision of the expenditures, whether it is not the duty of some official of the Government to watch them, to examine and criticise them. We know well enough-it is human nature-that where a great number of men are employed in connection with a Government work, they are not always so careful as they should be in their expenditures. I notice quite a difference in the prices paid for articles in one province. I have been looking over the accounts, and I find, for instance, that for the Kentville farm, 215 bushels of oats were purchased from Cross and De Wolfe at 50 cents per bushel, while for the farm at Nappan, in the same province, 1,000 bushels of oats were purchased at 59 cents.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Were they purchased during the same season of the year?

There might be something in that, but what I want to know is whether the officers on the different farms are allowed to make purchases without regard to price. There is a large amount of money expended, and while we must assume that the department does its best to supervise these expenditures, I think criticism of this kind is useful. After all, it is our money, and we want to see that we get full value. ,

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. gentleman's criticism is perfectly fair criticism; every effort ought to be made to see that value is received for the expenditures. It is the duty of Mr. Grisdale, the Director of Experimental Farms, to visit every experimental farm at least twice a year, and he does so; some of them he visits more frequently. In addition, all the bills incurred at the different farms come here to Ottawa, are examined by the staff at the Experimental Farm, and are then sent to the Agricultural Department, where they are examined by the Accountant's Branch. I have no doubt that the Auditor General also pays some attention to them. Apparently, therefore, every care is taken to guard against improper prices being paid.
It appears to me to be a poor system of farming which necessitates the purchase of fodder, cereals, and vegetables in such large quantities.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It would be farming of a worse kind if the farms were fun.for commercial purposes.

There' is no doubt that
the experimental farms are doing useful work, but whether it is work most advantageous to the farmers I do not know. I know that the farm at Charlottetown, P.E.I.. is one of the best farms.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is a small farm.

Yes, but it is as large as the ordinary farm-sufficiently large, at any rate, to do good work. Under ordinary conditions, if a man cannot make a farm like that pay, there is surely something wrong in the management. There may be exceptional conditions on these, experimental farms. Some years ago, a gentleman named William Rennie, I think, came to our province to lecture on farming. I happened to be present at his meeting, and one of the first remarks he made was that he had gone on a farm belonging to the Ontario Government, ah ordinary farm with ordinary conditions, and had made it pay. As soon as he made that remark every farmer in the audience became interested. They wanted to know how he made it pay, and he went on to tell the story. Now, if we could do things like that, I believe it would do more good to the farming community than running farms at an enormous loss. I am not saying that these farms are not doing useful work, but somehow or other the farmers in my province have the idea that it is easy to farm when the Dominion Government is paying the bills. They would like to know how to make an ordinary-farm pay.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend must remember that an experimental farm is an entirely different proposition from a farm run as a commercial undertaking. I do not suppose that any experimental farm, where experiments and investigations are carried on, could be made to pay, so far as dollars and cents are concerned, though it does pay in other directions. I fancy my hon. friend has reference more particularly to the farm in Prince Edward Island. I am told that that is a small farm, only sixty acres in extent, on which stock experiments are being carried on. A considerable part of it is taken up with the growing of crops, cereals, and so on; .but if you are carrying on stock operations on any scale at all, if you have not sufficient room in which to produce enough hay for the feed of the stock, you have to buy outside. Perhaps the same state of affairs exists on the island. I do not know what sort of a hay farm it is, but naturally, being an experimental farm, a great deal of the land will have to be taken up for the growth of other things, and there will not be a great deal left for hay.
* For the administration and enforcement of the Destructive Insect and Pest Act, $75,000.

Before dinner the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Boulay) stated that there were not as many officers sent to inquire into the potato disease in Quebec as there were in New Brunswick. The minister made the reasonable explanation that there was not as much disease in Quebec as there was in New Brunswick. We are very much interested in that matter in Prince Edward Island. I understood that the department was trying to have the embargo removed from Canadian potatoes entering the United States, and that they were taking steps to convince the authorities of the United States that whatever disease there was in our potatoes was not of a serious character. I would like to know what has been done, and what prospects there are of having that embargo removed.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The embargo has been removed.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is no inspection of our potatoes going into the United States.
There must be something wrong about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Our potatoes are admitted to the United States without any Canadian inspection at all.

While there may not be a Canadian inspection, there is a very severe American inspection, which only takes place at a few isolated points, probably at Boston and somewhere in New York state. The places of inspection are so far away that our growers or merchants dare not take the chance of selling to the United States buyers because their shipments might be rejected.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My information from the deputy minister and the Entomologist of the department is that it is a matter of mere form in the United States, and that it is not serious in any way.
That may be so at the present time, but it was not so a month ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My information is that the importer of potatoes in the United States gets a permit for taking them in, and that permit names the point at which they will be inspected. The assurance to the Department of Agriculture here from the Department of Agriculture in the United States is to -the effect that the inspection will be of a very ordinary character, and that there will be no shutting out of our potatoes unless it is evident that they are. affected with a serious disease. If they are only reasonably affected by disease they will be passed.
What ports will be available to Maritime Province shippers? [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They will specify them in the permit.
As a matter of fact, what port do they specify?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They will consider the convenience of the importer. They do not restrict it to any special port, but they will name the port that suits the convenience of the man, one of their own citizens, who is importing the potatoes.
Then, as far as the Maritime Provinces are concerned,, Boston would be the port of entry in nearly every case.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

Up to five or six weeks ago the conditions of these inspections were so severe that merchants in New Brunswick could hardly take the responsibility of sending potatoes down there because in many cases what they considered to be a perfectly good article would be condemned

when it got to Boston, and, after they had paid the freight and duty, they would have nothing left. In many cases they were called upon to make good a shortage.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There has not been much movement to the United States lately, because the price has been so high at home.
No, the price in Canada has been abnormally high and the crop has been very light. Yet the price in the United States is little better than it is in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is now.

It has been during the
whole season except on two occasions and for two or three days at a time. If the road were perfectly open, you could be assured that, if our farmers could get the benefit of the extra 10 per cent, they would do so. One reason why the farmer has not got the extra price is because the inspection has been so onerous that he dare not take the chance. I do not know that this Government could accomplish anything. I am only pointing the situation out to the minister, and I realize that he is not the minister of the department, and I therefore do not expect him to answer these questions readily. But, if something could be done by the department to get them to throw the door a little wider open so as to make it an ordinary commercial transaction, it would be a great benefit to the farmers of the Maritime Provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
T'he minister took this matter up personally. He went to Washington and saw Mr. Houston, the Agricultural Secretary, at Washington, and as a result the following regulations were promulgated:
Shipment of Potatoes to United States.
On and after the 1st January, 1916, potatoes may be shipped from Canada to the United States, subject to the following conditions:
(1)	Potatoes offered for export to the United States must be free from injurious diseases and insect nests.
(" Injurious diseases and insect pests " shall not apply to diseases common and widespread in both Canada and the United States, but in the case of even such common and widespread diseases the stock offered for shipment shall be reasonably free from infection, with such diseases.)
(2)	No shipment may be made until a permit has been issued to the United States importer as provided for in the United States regulations. Each shipment should therefore be designated on the accompanying papers by the number which will be furnished by the United States importer.
Inspection will be made by a United States inspector at the port of entry specified in the
permit, and if the shipment be found to be diseased, entry may be refused.
(3) No inspection or certification will be required prior to shipment, but potato growers and shippers are advised that the continuation of such entry will depend on the offering for entry into the United States of potatoes free from dangerous diseases and insect pests.
All persons engaged in this trade should have their potatoes carefully " racked," and any diseased or scabby potatoes removed.
For further information, apply to the Dominion Botanist, Central Experimental Farm, Ottawa.
Published by the direction of the Hon. Martin Burrell, Minister of Agriculture, Ottawa, December 27, 1915.	-
In the view of the department the restrictions are not onerous in any way. The minister has done everything he possibly could, but if there is any more that can be done I am sure he will gladly do it.

These regulations may be all right from the point of view of the department. But they are not farmers; they only think they are farmers. They do not know the difficulty of tilling the soil and of trying to make the farm pay the bills. To the practical farmer, however, these regulations seem altogether impracticable. The potato business is handled in . carload lots. A man in Boston may wire: " Can you Ship me five or ten cars of potatoes to-morrow?" The merchant replies: " I can, or I cannot, at such and such a price." Now, if these potatoes were going from China to British Columbia it would be all right. In that case you would know exactly who was the owner, and who was the consignee, and just where the potatoes were to be inspected. There would be plenty of time. But in the case of this shipment of potatoes to Boston, one does not know at what point the potatoes will be stopped. They may be stopped at Portland, or go on to Boston, or be turned off to Lowell or some other place in the States. If the purchaser has to make all these arrangements before he can get a carload of potatoes, it will absolutely tie up the business. Why, the market may change ten cents a barrel in the meantime, and with a fluctuating market it is impossible to carry on business of this kind. These regulations may look all right on paper, but when applied to every-day business they improve conditions very little, if at all. Our potatoes go not only to Boston, but to all parts of the States. If we had them inspected at the nearest point it would be different. All potatoes from the Maritime Provinces have to go through

Vanceboro. If for some reason the inspector at Vanceboro should not pass the potatoes, they can be sent on to Montreal or Toronto; but, if you are going to have the potatoes inspected at Boston, you may lose the whole shipment if the inspector turns you down there, and they will do it with

out any reason whatever. The risks are so great that the ordinary merchant will not take chances.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend lives in a district where the potato is a very important item of commerce, and, consequently has a more intimate acquaintance with the business than I have. But I am informed by the officers of the department that these regulations not only read all right, 'but work all right. In fact, since they were promulgated the department has not had a single complaint, and if there had been any complaints we should have heard of them from our inspectors, who are moving around the country.
When did these regulations go into effect?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: On the 1st of January, 1916. I can understand that there might be a case in which it would be more convenient for a shipper to have his potatoes inspected at Vanceboro than at Boston, but that is a matter which rests with the Government of the United States, and they ha-re evidently taken the view that they ought to be guided by the wishes of the men to whom they grant the permit to bring potatoes into the United States. I do not- see that it would make very much difference to the man importing, whether the potatoes were inspected at Vanceboro or at Boston, except that Boston is a large potato centre, and that might make some difference. But, as I said before, we have not receivea a single complaint from any of the shippers in the whole country.

I am speaking from my own personal knowledge. I raise a few potatoes myself. On the 1st of January I had about two carloads of potatoes in the warehouse. I naturally wanted as good a price as I could get for them. I found that the Boston price was a little higher than the price in Montreal or Toronto. I was in touch with a commission merchant in Boston, a friend of mine, who would handle the shipment for me. I went to some merchants in Canada with whom I was well acquainted and they all advised me not to ship to Boston; they said they had tried it them-

selves, but the regulations were so onerous that it was too risky. The result was that I sold my two carloads in Canada. I got $3 a barrel for them.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: More than you would have got in Boston.

I am not finding fault
with the price. I think I got more than they were worth. But those were the facts in my own case.

The hon. member for
Carleton (Mr. Carvell) has mentioned some difficulties in connection with shipping potatoes by land to the United States. But the man who ships by water has even greater difficulties. When shipping potatoes from Prince Edward Island we usually send them by schooner; whereas a carload takes about 600 bushels, a schooner takes about 6,000 bushels or more; and the larger the quantity uf course the greater the risk. The embargo on potatoes has not made any difference in the last two years, because the price in )the United States was low and our own price was just about the same level. However, in some year it might happen that there was a short crop in the United States and a big crop in Canada, and then the privilege of exporting potatoes to the United States would be of considerable advantage. If such a condition should arise, the time would be too short to make new regulations, and I think the regulations should be made in advance to provide for such a contingency. I presume that the Agricultural Department at Washington made these changes in view of representations that our potatoes had no disease. It would be a good thing if we could g<!t that fact established and the embargo removed. The risk would then not be so great. Anybody in the shipping business will understand this at once.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The embargo is removed.
But the inspection is still there.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Of course, it is their own
inspection and made for their own purposes.

If that could be removed and we could get back to the conditions that prevailed four or five years ago, it would be much better. Anybody in the shipping business will understand that no person could take the risk of sending a cargo of potatoes from Prince Edward Island, for instance, to Boston, with the possibility of having them turned down. Potatoes are a perishable article and the

cargo would prove a total loss if rejected by the inspector. We should be very little worse off if the embargo were still there. If an arrangement could be made under which the United States authorities would accept the certificate of some official in Canada or at the port of export, that would overcome the difficulty. If that cannot be done, of course it cannot be helped. But unless some such arrangement can be made, no shipper will take the chance of having a cargo oi potatoes thrown back on his hands, and no business will be done.

I am not going to make any recriminations about the army of inspectors that travel around the country. These positions were a godsend to some of the smaller office-seekers. When one of the faithful got a little ugly, they could make him a potato inspector, and thus an easy way was afforded out of a good many political difficulties.
No responsibility.

No responsibility, and a good salary; and not only that but no requirement in the way of knowledge-anybody could be a potato inspector. The whole thing was a farce and made no difference whatever except that it cost the country a lot of money. I would like to know how many of these inspectors are still employed. There are two gentlemen at least living in New Brunswick, and holding these positions, and so far as we can see they receive the same salaries as last year and do nothing. We had them by the. dozen last year. How many are there left, and what are their names?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The inspectors employed
at present under' the Destructive Insect and Pest Act are: J. R. Brownlee, P. R. Cowan, B.S.A., W. O. Johnston, George Partridge, Sydney G. Peppin, and R. Tre-9 p.m. panier. These men were engaged during the summer conducting field inspection of potatoes and demonstrating simple control measures for potato diseases, which have caused considerable economic loss throughout the Maritime Provinces. On some 450 farms the removal of diseased hills of potatoes was inaugurated and carried on by the farmers under the supervision of the inspectors, with results that were satisfactory at harvest time. The quality of potatoes harvested by these farmers exceeded anything they had harvested before. In addition, potato spraying demonstrations were held at a large number of farms since it is found that . late
blight causes incalculable damage. From a careful examination, diseases were found to prevail causing losses as follows: Black leg, 7 per cent loss, 840,000 bushels; Rhizoc-tonia, 5 per cent loss, ot 600,000 bushels; mosaic disease, 10 per cent loss, or 1,200,000 bushels; late blight, 25'per cent, or 3,000,000 bushels; total of 47 per cent, or 5,640,000 bushels. A general statement from Prince Edward Island shows that the losses due to late blight in 1915, when it was particularly severe, amounted to not less than 2,000,000 bushels of potatoes. Both these estimates entirely neglect the consequential loss resulting from diseases during storage, which, on the average, amount to 17 per cent of the tubers in storage. It will be evident that there was urgent need of a systematic educational campaign with a view to the eradication of these excessive losses. The inspectors, under the direction of Messers. Murphy and Cunningham, carried on spraying demonstrations in the farms in their several districts. The Tesult was gratifying. The crop gave a return of 97 bushels an acre on the average over that of the unsprayed fields, while in one case 113 bushels an acre were harvested after being sprayed by inspectors over the crop from neighbouring unsprayed fields. Furthermore, the inspectors carried on experiments at four farms relating to the control of powdery scab. These plots had to be planted, manured, treated .and sprayed up to 'harvest time, and to be harvested in order to collect the necessary data. Already these experiments have revealed that certain chemical substances had a decided beneficial influence on the control of this scab. The inspectors also assisted in the work commenced on the reestablishment of the Gar.net Chile industry for the Bermuda market, a problem of much economic importance to Nova Scotia districts. These and other field experiments resulted in the production of a superior grade of potatoes. During winter the inspectors continued seed selections on the farms where experiments were carried on, as well as on those from which diseases were eliminated by demonstrating to the farmers. This preliminary work, essential for the securing of good seed strains, was found very necessary; and the result of this work will surely show up next harvest when potatoes of a quality, purity and freedom from diseases are available as never before. A study of 115 varieties of potatoes grown in New Brunswick was also commenced, and selections are being made of

varieties particularly resistant to certain diseases. The study of these varieties is now being continued under the direction of the Dominion botanist by Mr. Cowan, also an inspector. Up to date, the time for the inspector has not only been very fully and usefully occupied but additional work in other directions, is proposed in the coming year which would make the retention of the six inspectors now employed very necessary. The work covers fully the provinces of Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, Quebec and New Brunswick. The work on the elimination of potato diseases, already begun, it is contemplated, will be continued next year in order to be prepared for the keeping open of. foreign *markets of consequence to the growers, particularly under the new agreement with the United States.

The minister's statement is another statement that looks nice on paper-but that is about all there is to it. The fact is, there has never been a poorer potato crop in the Maritime Provinces in seven or eight years than there was last year, notwithstanding that we had this army . of inspectors. All this talk about powdery scab is sheer moonshine. The Government employed, an entomologist at a large salary simply for the purpose of going down to New Brunswick and preventing the farmer from getting the price for his potatoes that he ought to get. I say the Government should be condemned for that, and the entomologist should be fired.

What does the hon. gentleman call this disease in the potatoes?
Mr. CARVELL; There is no disease.
What do you call this scab?
Scab, of course; that is what it has been called ever since you and I were born.
I suppose it is hereditary?

You will always find a few potatoes with scab upon them. As for powdery scab, that is all moonshine. The fact that it is all nonsense was the reason why the Unted States Government removed the embargo.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The result of these investigations caused the United States to do that.

These gentlemen went around the country a year ago and condemned the potatoes of a large proportion *of the farmers in my county, because, as they said, they were full of powdery scab. But I can produce men-by the dozen I was going to say-who planted the very potatoes that these scientific gentlemen pronounced, as being badly affected with powdery scab, and you never saw cleaner or better potatoes in your life than were grown from them. I can produce men right in my constituency who will make affidavit to that effect. This talk about powdery scab is just another means of finding places for political friends who want to earn their living without working. This question of spraying potatoes is better known among the farmers of New .Brunswick than if is among the officers of this department. At no place' on the American continent has potato growing reached as high a state of efficiency as it has along the St. John river in the province of New Brunswick and across the line-in the state of Maine. I think it is the opinion of most farmers in the Maritime Provinces that spraying with the Bordeaux mixture is usually productive of good. They claim that it removes the fungus growth, or what is usually called. rust. When I was home the last week in January I discussed this matter with a gentleman who told me that he had sprayed his potato plants six or seven times during the summer. The spraying is done with a machine costing over $100; as the machine-goes along, the spray is automatically pumped under the leaves and -stalks of. the plant. He said that he sprayed the whole field of potatoes with the .exception of half a dozen rows, and that when he came to dig them he had a better yield from the -half-dozen tows- than he had from the rest of the field, which he had sprayed.
I want to be fair in this matter; I will give both sides of the case. A gentleman from Floreneeville told me that he sprayed all but half a dozen tows, and that he got better results from the sprayed portion than from the portion which he had not sprayed; so, you have evidence both ways. In my judgment the spraying does good. But the farmer knows that; he does not need any information on that subject from the inspectors or from the Department of Agriculture. Last year I did not spray the plants, and I got just as good a crop as my neighbours did; perhaps I will use the spray next year, because I think it might

do some good. It is an insult to the farmers of New Brunswick for these inspectors to go around the country and presume to teach the farmers how to raise potatoes. This entomologist held a meeting in my town, with the Commissioner of Agriculture in New Brunswick, and they preached that there was nothing in the world but powdery scab, and that it would have to be eradicated. They had some of the men so scared that they would not allow the inspectors on the premises for fear they would poison them over this question of powdery scab. This same entomologist had another meeting down there within the last three or four months, and they say that there is no powdery scab, and never was any. That is what the Secretary of Agriculture for New Brunswick says. There never was any powdery scab; the whole thing was a farce from the beginning. Let us get rid of these inspectors: the farmers do not want them; they are no good. Let the farmers go on in their own way; they know how to raise potatoes. Several thousand dollars will be saved, and there will be an advantage to the minister, because he will not have so many applications from office-seekers.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have not been pressed by people seeking positions as inspectors. I do not think that any one ever came to me asking to be appointed to inspect the potatoes of New Brunswick. With regard to powdery scab, an embargo was placed upon Canadian potatoes going into the United States because it was claimed by the advisers of the Agricultural Department of the United States that powdery scab existed very largely in the province of New Brunswick. That impression has been removed, largely through the action of the Minister of Agriculture, who was able to fortify his position by the information that he received from the inspectors who investigated this matter. If we had not had a scientific-man to investigate this subject and make report, I doubt very much whether the Department of Agriculture of the United States could have been persuaded to lift the embargo. They have not only removed the embargo, but have admitted that powdery scab did not exist to the extent that they believed it did, and that it was not sufficiently dangerous to justify the placing of an embargo. Our potatoes are now subject simply to inspection by somebody in the United States, whereas, when the embargo prevailed, arrangements were made by which the potatoes were inspected in Canada by Canadian inspectors. I do.not
see how the Agriculture Department or its inspectors were in any way responsible for the placing of this embargo upon our potatoes. The people in the United States may have been actuated by the best of good faith when they expressed the belief that this alleged disease was dangerous, but they have practically admitted their error since then.
Mr. HUGHES': When was it that representations were made to the United States that there was no disease in our potatoes?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Representations were made to them from the beginning. I think it was some time last fall, in November, that the Minister of Agriculture got this undertaking from Mr. Houston.

That, no doubt, is the
explanation which has been given to my hon. friend the acting minister. This idea about powdery scab was got up not in Washington, but in the town of Caribou, in the state of Maine. When the potato growers and dealers of the county of Aroostook found that under the Wilson tariff potatoes were practically on the free list, a duty of only about 10 per cent being left on them, they said: "We have got to stop those Canadian potatoes from getting in here." And they started out. I know the man's name, I know the combination, the gentleman who started the proposition. They sent a lot of detectives down to New Brunswick, who claimed they found powdery scab.' Then there was a big outcry and the matter was carried to Washington. Delegates from all over the United States went to Washington. I think the Deputy Minister of Agriculture was there. There were 500 delegates, all protesting against the importation of Canadian potatoes because of powdery scab. Then the Dominion entomologist went to Woodstock-it was more of a political meeting than anything else -and met the Secretary of Agriculture of New Brunswick. They decided that the country was full of powdery scab. They appointed their horde of inspectors, who went around the country up till last May, and stopped shipment after shipment of potatoes because they said they were affected with powdery scab. Every officer of this department and of the department in New Brunswick was protesting that this country was simply alive with powdery scab, and these inspectors were refusing the farmers the right to sell potatoes because of it. Then, when the United States Government became ashamed of the trans-

action, these same gentlemen came round and said there was no powdery scab. Now the minister says there is no powdery scab, and the Secretary of Agriculture for New Brunswick says there never was any powdery scab. It only shows the utter nonsense of the whole transaction. The thing has simply been worked-I do not know whether it was for political jobs or not, but it looks as if that was all there was to it. However, we have demonstrated that the powdery scab was only a farce to start with. The potatoes are all right, and if the minister will use his good offices with the Department of Agriculture of the United States I hope he can have these ridiculous regulations removed, so that the trac^e may go on, subject to the little duty imposed on potatoes entering the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend may be sure that the Minister of Agriculture will do all he can-he is intensely anxious to do all he can-to help the potato growers and all agriculturists.
Mr. .1. J. HUGHES: The minister is not acquainted with all the facts, or at least he has not stated them to the committee, with regard to this potato business. When the Wilson Administration came into office in the United States, the duty on potatoes was reduced to 10 per cent, ad valorem, to all countries in the world. Under the reciprocity arrangement proposed between Canada and the United States, we would have had the privilege of exporting potatoes to that country, and no other country would have had that privilege. But in consequence of the Underwood tariff potatoes began to come in freely in the autumn of 1912 from Great Britain and Germany, ,and, as the officers of the Department of Agriculture well know there is -a very dangerous disease in Europe known as canker. The United States authorities became alarmed lest, on account of these heavy importations from Europe, that disease might be introduced into their country, and a convention was called at Washington to take the whole matter into consideration. The department here sent to that convention an officer who stated that Canadian potatoes were diseased, and so he assisted the people of the United States in puting an embargo on potatoes. Since' that was done and since it was brought to the attention of the department how serious a mistake they had made and how greatly they had injured this country

by restricting the exportation of potatoes, they have been trying to have that embargo removed, and have been telling the people of the United States that we have practically no disease. Well, repentance is better than continuance in error.
In sin.

Or in sin. It is repentance. But we have been seriously injured by it, and it will be difficult to get the regulations removed. I quite agree with what has been said by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell), that this whole thing was largely a farce, and that the disease existed only in the imagination of these inspectors, for some reason or other. The farmers down in my province have proved that bejond shadow of doubt. The inspectors either did not know their business or they had some object in view that we cannot understand. As a matter of fact, I know the farm to which two inspectors went in the autumn of 1912. That was the farm of a large grower of potatoes. They inspected his cellar, reported that his potatoes were diseased, and told him that under no condition must he use those potatoes for seed; that he must get clean seed or otherwise he would have no potatoes; that he would not only ruin himself but injure his neighbours He was a practical man and knew that there was nothing the matter with his potatoes-that they had no disease. They were the same that year as they had been for forty years. There was some scab but, as my hon. friend says, you will hardly get a field of potatoes without a few scabby ones. He went on and planted those potatoes, he got seed from them for two years, and two years afterwards the inspectors came, inspected his potatoes, and gave him a clean bill of health. He was the only man in the settlement who had no disease in his potatoes. In the face of facts like that, known to everybody in the settlement and in neighbouring settlements, it is absolutely no use for the inspectors to be sent down. I seriously advise the Minister of Agriculture, if he has no use for these men, to see the Militia Department and get them to go to the war.
I believe that Artemus Ward wanted to send all his wife's relations to the war. The farmers of Prince Edward Island want to see all these gentlemen go to the war. They might do some good there, but they are certainly an injury to the agricultural industry of this country.
There are a number of other professors or

lecturers who go around telling the farmers how to farm. They may have been in college and have learned the Latin names of vegetables and plants, but -they know very, very little about practical farming- and since the present Government came into power their numbers have been increased and they seem to grow less wise. Bums has described men of this kind by saying that they go into colleges sticks and come out asses. There are a great number of them in the Agricultural Department. I shall tell the Deputy Minister of Agriculture, who understands farming, I presume, what I heard one of these men say at a meeting. He was telling the farmers how to farm. A number of farmers attended the meeting-not a great number attend them in my province now. This lecturer invited questions. One farmer asked him how he would bring on some worn-out fields on the back of his farm. He had no manure, and ' as this was a professor who could give information on any subject, he asked him what he should do. And do you kn'ow the answer he got? Sow clover. Now, any practical man who has ever farmed at all knows that you must have the land in good cultivation before you can get a catch of clover. To sow clover in worn-out land-why, you *might as well sow it on the seashore. After that, nobody paid any attention to . what he said. That was the kind of man who was sent down there to tell the people how to farm. Surely something can be saved by putting these men on to some other work. The number going around the country is very large. I heard one member from the province of Quebec ask the minister to send some one through that province-send them to' Quebec, send them anywhere, but do not send them to Prince Edward Island.

I was very much impressed by the statement "made by my hon friend from Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) in reference to the inspection of potatoes. I must confess *I have not had a great deal of experience in the potato business, although we grow a great many potatoes for export in and around m'y constituency. But it seemed to me, from What my hon. friend from Carleton said in regard to the inspectors in and around that portion of New Brunswick, that some of his costituents have a reasonable ground for complaint against the Department of Agriculture. A practical illustration will enable the committee to understand the condition of affairs better than
*anything I could say. This gentleman-I forget his name, I think he came from Victoria county-sold a carload of potatoes last spring to a gentleman in my county-in fact, in my parish. Whether the potatoes *were good or bad I am not in a position to tell the committee definitely; but they came to Sackville by rail, and, for some reason or other, whether proper or not, the consignee refused to accept them, declaring that they were not up to the standard of the potatoes he had paid for. He had purchased the potatoes under a written contract, and a Clause in the contract was to the effect that the potatoes must be inspected and passed by the inspector of potatoes in that locality. The shipper of the potatoes loaded his potatoes, and the inspector deputed a man to inspect them. The potatoes were given a clean bill of health by the sub-inspector, and, as I have said, they were shipped to the consignee in Sackville. When they arrived there the consignee would not accept them, and they remained on the track for some days or weeks, until eventually the officials of the Intercolonial Railway sold them to pay for demurrage and freight. They were purchased by a number of people around Sackville -for as low as eighteen cents, twenty cents, and twenty-five cents a bushel. According to the information which I received from the gentleman who purchased them, they were excellent potatoes. A lawsuit resulted, the gentleman in Victoria country, or Carleton county, suing the consignee for .the price of the carload of potatoes. The case was tried in the court at Dorchester a couple of months ago. I ,was not engaged in the case. Mr. Hartley, I believe, acted for the gentleman from Victoria county, and his client happened to come to my office to get subpoenas for some of the witnesses who had purchased the potatoes, and I heard the story. The seller of the potatoes lost his case, because it turned out that the man who inspected them was a subinspector appointed by the real inspector, and a man not legally qualified to inspect. Therefore the bill of health which he had granted was of no use; the judge withdrew the case from the jury, and the Victoria gentleman lost the value of his carload of potatoes because of the neglect and carelessness of the potato inspector in my hon. friend's constituency. I do not know whether the system of inspection is conducted properly generally, but I think that that man who suffered loss by the neglect

and carelessness of the inspector has an equitable claim upon the Government to be recouped.
Was the inspector himself present?*
I do not know whether he was there or not; the judge ruled that he had no authority to appoint a sub-inspeotor.
The inspector may have been sick, and many have appointed some one to act in the emergency.
Why should the inspector appoint a man who was not legally qualified to make the inspection?
Does the hon, gentleman undertake to say that in other respects the plaintiff's action was well founded? Had he a written contract?

Yes, he had a written contract. I ,do not wish to mislead the committee in any way. I do not know what the jury might have done if the case had gone before them, but the judge withdrew the case on the legal point that the seller had not fulfilled part of the contract be-oause he had not received a proper certificate of inspection from Ihe real inspector.
Were the potatoes perfectly good?
Perfectly good.

Were they pronounced
excellent by those who bought them?
Yes.
And there was no suggestion that the purchasers could have inspected the carload and found the potatoes good?
That was the evidence of the people who purchased the potatoes.

My hon. friend from
Perth (Mr. Morphy) does not understand the situation. The whole inspection was a farce; that is the difficulty. It is not as if the Government appointed technical experts from Ottawa or from some of the colleges. There are a few inspectors of that class, but the ordinary inspector is simply some fellow who was out of a job.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Does the hon. gentleman
contend that it is the duty of the inspectors appointed by the Government to inspect potatoes sold by a gentlemen in Carleton county to a gentleman in Westmorland county?

That is the whole
trouble.
That was part of the contract. [DOT]

The whole trouble is that the Government appoint any fellow out of a job who has enough political pull to get the position. The inspectors themselves look upon the whole thing as a farce. They say: "this is a farce anyway; it does not make any difference whether we sign that paper, or get some one else to sign it." The inspector referred to appointed some one else; the matter got into the law courts, and unfortunately there was a condition in the contract which made inspection necessary before the seller could have a right of action. Therefore the two men-the man who was appointed by the Government and the man whom he appointed as sub-agent-had the same knowledge, or, rather, I should say, neither of them had any. Unfortunately, the wrong man signed the document; that was the trouble.
For the development of the dairying industries, and the improvement in transportation, sale and trade in food and other agricultural products, $155,000.

Is this the item out of
which Mr. Ruddick's salary is paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No; Mr. Ruddick's salary
is paid out of the Civil Government Estimates of the Department of Agriculture. All the salaries are paid out of the Civil Government vote.
Well, the staff will be paid out of this?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No, the salaries are paid
out of Civil Government Estimates.

Would the minister explain, then, just what this $155,000 is to be expended for?
Mr. .HAZEN: This item is for the development of the dairying industry and improvement in transportation, sale and trade in food and other agricultural products. The amount spent last year was $215,910. The Estimate is made up this year as follows:
Headquarters	$15,250
Dairy division	 97,150
Markets	 21,790
Cold storage service	 20,800
These items are subdivided again in this way:	The expenses of headquarters and
branch offices, consisting of printing, stationery, contingencies, unforeseen expenses; Montreal office, rent, water rates, telephone, and incidental expenses; Halifax office,

rent, telephone, etc. Dairy division-inspectors of dairy products, cheese and butter weighing and cow testing, dairy recorders, dairy stations, apparatus for experiments, supplies and repairs and experimental cold storage warehouse at Grimsby. Markets division-inspectors at Montreal, Portland, Halifax and in Great Britain, and temporary employees at Montreal. Cold storage branch-cream cold storage bonus, travelling expenses, cold storage inspector, and items of this sort. I do not suppose my horn friend wants me to go into all these details.
What is the explanation of the $21,000 for markets?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: These are the items making up the expenditure of $21,790: Permanent employees in Canada-cargo inspector at Montreal, $1,500; cargo inspectors at Montreal, Portland and Halifax-
I am not so much interested in the items, but I wo\ild like to have an explanation of what is done in the way of looking for markets for our agricultural products.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Cargo inspectors are stationed at Montreal, Quebec, Halifax, Liverpool, Bristol, and, in the winter season, at Portland, Maine, to report on the conditions of all perishable goods delivered to and discharged from steamships, and to supervise the handling generally of these products. A large number of selfrecording thermometers and thermostats are used, and thousands of records are available. A Canadian shipper may, by application to the Dairy and Cold Storage Commissioner, secure complete records of any consignments from the time the goods arrive at the loading port in Canada until they are distributed in the United Kingdom. This applies also, but not so generally, t<\ shipments to South Africa and Australia. They also supervise the refrigerator car services.

A little over a month ago all the members of the House-at least I did-got notice from the department that the report of the Dairy Commissioner had been issued and that we could receive it by going to the distributing office. When we went there we found that the report was not available, and it was not available for ten days, or quite a time after that. My information is that' the report that had been issued was called in and that a new
report was issued. Perhaps the minister would give an explanation.
' Mr. HAZEN: My information is that the report as prepared in the first instance, and before it had been distributed, contained, references to certain matters in connection with the war, the publication of which would have been entirely against public policy and public interest at the present time. That was eliminated from the report.
Would the minister state what the substance of the report was?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No; it might as well be printed in the report and circulated as that I should tell it to the House.

My information is not exactly the same as the information the minister has. My information is that there were references to the sale of certain articles, but that after something had taken place in the House in connection with the sale of hay, this report was recalled. I notice in the index of the report that the first item is " War Office Agency." There is nothing whatever in the report about a War Office agency. A new report has been issued, but, as is usual in most shady transactions, care was not taken to cover up all the tracks. They forgot to take the index out of the new report. The index contains the reference "War Office agency," but there is absolutely nothing in the report in connection with the War Office agency. We have here a report with the first leaf cut out and another leaf pasted in. Any one can see that it is of absolutely different paper and different type. The sheet has obviously been pasted in. I am afraid the explanation given by the minister is not the right one. My information is that, afteT the discussion which the Minister of Agriculture and the hon. member for Car-leton had in the House over hay about a month ago, it was found necessary to cut this sheet out. I think the minister should give us some better explanation than. he has given.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have given the explanation that was made to me. It occurs to me that what the hon. gentleman says confirms my explanation. He says that in the second book the index contains the reference "War Office agency," and that there is nothing in the report itself bearing on that subject The index has probably

been overlooked. That bears out the information that was given to me, which was to the effect that it was thought inimical to the public interests to publish what appeared in the first Teport, with regard to supplies that were being bought by the department for the British and Allied Governments.

It would be pretty hard to make me believe that the gentleman in charge of getting out this report did not know what would be inimical to the public interests. He would know perfectly well what to put in the report and what to leave out. The fact is that after certain statements had been made in this House it was thought necessary to recall the first report, and take out this leaf. I feel certain of that.

The silence of my hon. friend is very ominous. It seems to me that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) has put a pretty straight proposition to the minister this evening. He practically says that he does not believe the explanation given by the minister. He does not mean that personally, of course.
I also want to add my testimony to the ability and knowledge and good judgment of the gentleman who submits this report. To my knowledge, he has been in the department for thirteen or fourteen years, and I think even longer than that. He has been making reports every year for the department, and I believe has been doing good work for Canada. I have nothing more to say about him. I do not believe he would put in one word that was inimical to the interests of this country, or one word that would help our enemies, or one word that would not be in the interests of the people of Canada who pay for the production of these reports and the salaries of the officials who are producing them. My information is that the only thing that has been taken out of the report was a statement to the effect that the department had purchased large quantities of hay, oats and flour. This was in" accordance with the satisfactory method adopted [DOT] by the Government at the time of the South African war; that is to say, to put in the report just a general statement of purchases. All that is entirely innocent and perfectly correct. But hon. gentlemen will remember that there was a discussion in the House on the . 25th and 27th of January last, during which I narrated some of the conditions in the prov-. 
ince of New Brunswick in regard to hay purchases by the Agricultural Department. The Minister replied on the 27th, and I am very sorry he is not here to-night. I am not going into this subject now because I hope to have an opportunity of discussing it with the minister when he is in the House again. But as the present Acting Minister of Agriculture was the man responsible for the difficulty, I might address him. I went to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and pointed out to him the iniquity that was being practised in my province and county. I said that if he would give a contract to McCain, who had the only compressing plant in Canada not in use at the time, or anybody else who would furnish some competition, I would be satisfied. That was followed by a letter addressed fio Mr. Ruddick, dated December 24, offering to pay for loose hay not less than $15 per ton if they would give a contract for from 3,000 to 5,000 tons. But they Tyould not do it, and the acting minister knows why they would, not do it. I had a conversation with the minister, and I am sorry we had a little disagreement as to the exact words used. We did not disagree with regard to the substance, however. I told the minister that if he would give McCain or any other responsible firm a contract, in order to furnish some competition, I would be satisfied and nothing more would be said about it. But instead of doing that, the minister came to this House and read an old agreement which was made with a company with whom I was connected fourteen years ago, when I was a private citizen, not a member of the legislature or a member of the House of Commons. This document, which was public property all over New Brunswick for years, was prepared in the presence of every hay dealer in the county. While there was a clause in the agreement restricting the price to the farmer,., my hon. friend should have known that the contract could never have been filled without that clause in it. Smith demanded and was perfectly right in insisting on the clause being put in. He was signing a contract to furnish us with four thousand tons of hay. He said: "I am selling you 4,000 tons of hay at a certain price. If Bohan is allowed to go around the country buying hay and paying more than I can afford, I cannot fill my contract, and I want to be protected against that." Bohan Brothers were members of the parent company and might purchase without profit,

so we put the clause in. Bohan and all the other hay merchants present agreed to it. They knew all about it. It was put in at Smith's request.

What clause does my
hon. friend refer to?
That the farmer should not receive more than $8 a ton.

And in case more than
$8 a ton was paid he should be fined.
Sit down, if you please. I do not know whether the farmer was to be fined. This thing has been public in New Brunswick for years.
Did the hon. gentleman draw up that agreement?

I helped to sign it. I
take my full share of responsibility.
You have to.

I do. I never go hack on anything I do, and I never say a thing behind a man's back that I would not. say to his face. I say that that clause was perfectly right from Smith's standpoint. If it had not been in the agreement, it is quite true that Bohan might have offered a larger price for a few lots of hay in each community, and Smith would then have to pay a greater price than he could afford.

And the farmers would have benefited to that extent.
Mr., CARVELL: The farmer was getting $1.50 a ton more than he ever got in his life before.
He must be getting $5 or $6 more at the present time.

He is, and even then he is not getting within $1.50 of what he ought to get, and, when I started into this 'business he was not getting within $3 of what he ought to get. As I said, the clause was put in at Smith's request and for his protection. I asked the minister to give the contract to Mr. McCain, or some other responsible firm who would give us some competition, and in that case I would have nothing more to say. The minister did not say whether he would or would not, and at a subsequent conversation he said that he thought it was not possible. He said that he had given a contract to the Atlantic Hay company for 15,000 tons of hay, and that it was doubtful whether they could get more than that amount in New Brunswick, and that if a contract was given
to somebody else and they paid a higher price the Atlantic Hay company might not be able to fill their contract, and the department might be responsible to some extent. He did not think it would be fair and right. I want to tell this House what the acting minister knows better than any other man in Canada: he knows that he could not keep the lid on any longer; he knows that he had to give in. As the minister from New Brunswick he was compelled, not through my pressure, but through political pressure, to give a contract to another set of men, and I want to tell him that that 'hay compressing plant is in operation in .the town of Woodstock to-day, and the people of my constituency will get the competition which I urged the Government to provide some two months ago. If the Government had acted on my suggestion the matter would never have been discussed in this House, and it would not - have been necessary for my hon. friends opposite to mutilate a public document in order to get out of a difficulty in which they found themselves. The acting minister knows that, on account of a political rumpus in my constituency that threatened to rend the Conservative iparty in two, they were compelled to give a contract. Of course, the minister would not give it to McCain, for McCain is a Liberal, though he promised that he would pay the farmers $15 a ton for their hay. It was given to my hon. friend's friend, Smith, who has been buying at from $13 to $13.50 a ton. It is true that the only compressing plant that could carry on this business was owned by McCain in Woodstock. But he was a Liberal, and no amount of consideration for the public interest would drive the Minister of Agriculture to give the contract to a Liberal-that is a piece of political heresy that he has never been guilty of yet. But when the trouble got so bad that it threatened to split the 'Tory party in two, and when they came and said: Give us a contract or we will rebel; they gave a contract to a body of Conservatives. One of them is the police magistrate, a splendid gentleman, as the Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes) would say. Another is a lawyer; another a farmer; and two others are merchants. They are all good, responsible men-no fault to find with them. They purchased the McCain press; and they have got a contract, I do not know for how much. It was for 3,000 tons, but perhaps the minister will tell me the amount of it

now. And this concern is doing the very thing that I asked the minister to do two months ago, and which he refused. And, instead of meeting the charge I made, he read an ancient document to try and make a case against me. I notice that he did please some of his followers here, but he only made himself ridiculous in New Brunswick where the facts are known. The fact is, the pressure became so strong that he could not resist it and had to come to the proposition I made and do what I asked him-except that, instead -of giving the contract to the man who owned the p<lant and who had agreed to pay a good price to the farmer, he gave it .to political friends who bought the plant and who, so far as I know, did not agree to pay any particular price to the growers of the hay. But natural competition will run the price up, and the farmers will get a better price than they have been getting. This was done at the risk of a fight with Smith. They
10 p.m. went to St. John and Smith began to tell them:	We have
got Carvell licked. But these gentlemen said: " we are not here to lick Carvell, but we .are here to lick you if you don't give us contracts." They came to Ottawa and saw the minister, and the minister climbed down-not to help lick Carvell, but to save the other from a licking. That is an illustration of how things are being carried on by this department, and by this branch of the department. I find no fault with the officers; they are only the unfortunate medium through whom the dictates of the men behind the minister are carried out. I do not want to go any further now, but when I have an opportunity, later in the session, of discussing this matter with the minister. I shall have a few things more to say to him. For the present I am happy to tell the House and the country that the minister has been compelled to do the very thing I wanted him to do, except he has not done it nearly so well as it would have been done if he had taken my proposition. But my people will get the benefit of competition to some extent, and I hope they will get $15 a ton for their hay. Had I not interfered, they would have been selling to Smith for $12 and Smith would have cleaned up $75,000 instead of about $40,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No one knows better than my hon. friend that this discussion is absolutely out of order; but he has wanted an opportunity to make a statement to the House regarding this hay transaction, and, that being the case, I did not want to raise

a point of order, because I think nothing is gained in Committee of Supply by adhering too closely to the rule and confining the . discussion to the single item before the Chair. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) and the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) have talked of the " garbling " of the report. I made the statement supplied by the department as to what occurred, and I think that hon. gentlemen should have accepted that statement. They are not disposed to do so, and so I am obliged to say to the committee that [DOT] the suspicions of the hon. gentlemen are entirely unwarranted and unfounded. The change in the report had nothing to do with contracts for hay, or with any matters of that sort. That statement I make on the authority of the responsible officials of the department. I believe that statement to be true; I have no doubt of the truth of it.
The matter of the hay contract is pretty fresh in the minds of hon. members. We heard the attack made by the hon. member for Carleton on the Minister of Agriculture and we heard the minister's reply, and every one who heard that discussion knows that the Minister of Agriculture did not come off second best, but that he was able to maintain the position he had taken and to answer completely my hon. friend from Carleton. That hon. gentleman now is posing as the champion of the farmers of his constituency,- although- the minister showed the House that the hon. gentleman had not been so much the champion of the farmers in the past, but was ready to fine the farmers and punish them if they sold their hay for more than $8 a ton- not a very large sum to get for hay in the county of Carleton. But I do not intend to go into that, more especially as the hon. gentleman has indicated that he in-, tends to bring it up at a later day when the Minister of Agriculture is in the House. But I was not compelled by political or other considerations to take the^course he alleges I have taken. The estimate given to the department when the contract was entered into with the Imperial Hay Company-
The Atlantic Hay Company.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Atlantic Hay Company-I say the information in the possession of the department was that about 15,000 tons of the hay that would be required would be available from New Brunswick this year.

They awarded that contract for 15,000 tons. My hon. friend talks about Mr. Smith making from $60,000 to $75,000 out of the contract, but he knows that the final agreement was that Smith's books, or the books of the hay company, shall be open to the inspection of Government inspectors and accountants appointed by them, and that they shall not make a profit of more than $1 a ton on the hay they send out, the limit of which shall be $15,000, not $75,000, as stated by the hon. member for Carleton. The hon. gentleman sometimes talks in the language of exaggeration, but it is inexcusable for him to do so on this occasion, having in regard the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture concerning the agreement which was finally entered into. Every precaution was taken to see that everything was done regularly and in the proper manner. Now, what is the complaint cf the hon. member for Carleton? Some gentlemen from the county of Carleton made an application for another contract some weeks ago. They said they thought they [DOT]could supply 1,500 tons of hay, on the same terms and conditions as were contained in the agreement made with the hay company of which Mr. Smith and the Messrs. Peters are members. A contract was given these gentlemen, not for 1,500, but for 1,000 tons, because before they entered into the contract they said that that was all they would undertake to supply. In regard to my hon. friend's assertion that this is the first time that things were done contrary to the wishes of Mr. Smith, I desire to say that Mr. Smith had advised the department that he had no objection to offer if the contract was entered into with those gentlemen for the amount of hay which they said they were able to furnish. My understanding of the matter is that when it came to making the contract, they were willing to undertake to supply only 1,000 tons, intimating that perhaps at a later date, when they saw better how matters were and to what extent hay should be available in the country, they might be prepared to enter into a contract for the supplying of a further amount. The terms and conditions of this contract were the same as those of the agreement entered into with the other contractors, which provided that they could not make a profit of more than $1 a ton. I was not influenced by fear of schism in the Conservative party in Carleton county. They are good fighting men, as the Liberals in Carleton are, and when a contest comes they are prepared to stand together, more 90
strongly and more determinedly than they ever stood together in the past. The hon gentleman says that the facts are laughed at in New Brunswick. My information is of a very different character indeed. The greatest, possible interest has been taken in the matter, particularly in the hon. gentleman's constituency, where it is known that he is connected with the matter. If my information is correct, there is a feeling of indignation among the farmers in the county of Carleton over the publication of that contract which proposed to penalize and punish the farmers of the county for thinking of anything so iniquitous as selling their hay to any operator at more than $8 a ton. However, this is not the time and place to discuss this matter, although my hon. friend no doubt wanted an opportunity of making some reference to the debate that took place in which he and the Minister of Agriculture were the principal participants. I shall say nothing further about it at this time, except to assure the hon. member for Assiniboia and the hon. member for CaTleton, speaking in all sincerity, and having regard to the information which I have received, which I believe to be correct, that their suspicions with regard to what was in the report and what was afterwards deleted from it are absolutely without foundation.
I want to put my hon. friend right: it was not the farmer who might be penalized; it was the merchant.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
He would be penalized
for paying the farmer a little more.

It was not so bad for the Minister of Agriculture to make an argument of the kind advanced by my hon. friend to-night, bepause the minister did not know what he was talking about. The acting minister talks about this man Smith bringing his books into court, and about allowing him only $1 a ton profit. The minister will do mighty well if he does not pay $25 a ton for that hay instead of $23, because the most glorious set of books ever seen on earth will come before the minister. When you talk to the farmers in New Brunswick about Smith's books being brought before the minister or before a chartered accountant or inspector of the Government-well, my hon. friend is smiling; he knows the circumstances.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: 1 am smiling at my hon. friend.	.
At the time of the South African war, Conservatives could get contracts.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They say they could not.

There were a couple of gentlemen in the city of St. John by the name of Peters; I do not think my hon. friend will say they are not Conservatives. My hon. friend made a slip a few minutes ago, when he referred to the Atlantic Hay Company as the Imperial Hay Company. The Imperial Hay Company-that was the Peters' concern-had a contract in 1901-02. They were good Conservatives, and they got the contract on the basis upon which contracts were given to any one else. These gentlemen were quarter owners of the Atlantic Hay Company. B. F. Smith Carle-leton county, was a quarter-owner, A. C. Smith & Co. of St. John were quarter-owners, the Peters' were quarter owners, and a man named Macdonell of Montreal had a quarter. The Peters' have made up their minds . that the company has been badly handled from the political standpoint. There has been such a row that they have withdrawn from the company, and have sent circular notices to the trade to that effect. So you see, Mr. Chairman, that my hon. friend is having his own troubles in New Brunswick over this hay business.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No trouble.

There are some things that the hon. gentleman and I know which, perhaps, would not be interesting to the committee; therefore I shall not go into the matter any further. The history of the hay business in New Brunswick has not yet been half told. Possibly before we are a year older the minister and I may have another opportunity of enlightening the people a little on this wonderful question.
Arts and Agriculture-Fruit Branch, $115,000.

When I was referring to the powdery scab business, I made reference to the Dominion entomologist; I should have said, "Dominion botanist." I want to make that explanation, because, when I come to think it over, I know enough about technical terms to know that it was the botanist, not the entomologist, that I was after.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Under what circumstances did he say that?

It was at a dairymen's annual convention at Hemmingford. It is a practice that should not be allowed. That was just before the elections took place in British Columbia, and as the duty was put on not so much to help the apple-growers as to help the politicians and the Government of British Columbia, surely it is enough for .the politicians to engage in that class of work. There are enough of them, when you take both sides, to discuss that thoroughly, and if the Department of Agriculture has no departmental work for this official, would it not be a good idea to let him devote his time to politics and save that much money in this time of stress, when we want to practise the utmost economy? Can the Acting Minister of Agriculture, now that the elections are over, and apparently the extra duty has not been of much advantage to the British Columbia politicians, tell us whether it is proposed to take that duty off? '

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I dp not know the young man to whom my hon. friend refers, I can only assure my hon. friend that he had no instructions from me to go down and make any such statement, and I am quite satisfied that he got no instructions from any official occupying a position of responsibility in the department. It is not always safe, of course, to judge a man by a newspaper report of what he said. We all know that we often see reports of our speeches in newspapers that convey a different idea from what we had in mind. After all, a synoptic report is only the idea the reporter has of what the man says, and frequently the reporter's idea is incorrectly put into type. So a man's

speech is often misunderstood. I do not hesitate to say that no official of the department has a right to go into any part of the country and talk politics, and I will instruct the deputy minister to speak to Mr. Grindley about the matter. I am disposed to think that he may have referred to these duties as being of general assistance to the apple-growing industry, and it is quite likely that when we have the full text of his speech it will be seen that the synoptic report makes it convey a different meaning and that the speech which was actually made may not have been in any sense objectionable. As to the suggestion to change the tariff, I understand the resolutions will be before the House very soon, and that will be the time to discuss them.

I quite agree that it
would be quite possible that the gentleman was mis-reported, and also quite possible, and I think most likely, that if he did make reference to the tariff, it was without any intention to discuss political matters.
What is the present annual production of apples in British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The production for the last year was 650,000 boxes, which is equal to
1.000	cars. There are 3 boxes to a barrel.

I read a report from a
British Columbia paper to the effect that
30.000	acres were under orchard in British Columbia ,and that 40 per cent of that area was in bearing to a greater or less degree.,

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is about right, I am informed.

Has the department any
knowledge as to when the remaining 60 per cent will come into measurably full bearing?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They will all be in full
bearing in about ten years.

Can the department give any information as to the apple-growing industry in British Columbia, the kinds of apples grown, and whether they are making any advancement?	'
* Mr. HAZEN: My information is that they are growing a very superior class of apples in British Columbia.

That is a very illuminating answer, and I think we should let the item pass.
